question: In what order do the Activity lifecycle callbacks fire, and which one runs only once per instance?
answer:
An Activity is the entry point for one screen, and the system drives it through a fixed sequence of callbacks.

• onCreate(savedInstanceState) — Activity created. Inflate UI, restore state. Called ONCE per Activity instance.
• onStart — Activity becomes visible.
• onResume — Activity in foreground, receiving input.
• onPause — losing focus (another Activity in front, multi-window). Pause animations, save anything ephemeral. Called BEFORE onStop and BEFORE the next Activity's onResume.
• onStop — no longer visible.
• onRestart — coming back from stopped (after onStop, before onStart).
• onDestroy — Activity being torn down. Last call. Configuration changes recreate the Activity.
• onSaveInstanceState(out) — pre-onStop hook to save UI state into a Bundle (rotation / process death recovery).

Fragments mirror this with their own callbacks (`onAttach → onCreate → onCreateView → onViewCreated → onStart → onResume → onPause → onStop → onDestroyView → onDestroy → onDetach`).

A Compose-first app still has exactly one Activity, so the lifecycle is where you scope flow collection with `repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)` and where the process-death Bundle arrives.

question: What is a Fragment? When do you use Fragments vs Activities?
answer:
A Fragment is a reusable, self-contained piece of UI that lives inside an Activity (or another Fragment). Has its own lifecycle, view tree, and back stack support.

Use Fragments when:
• Multi-pane layouts (master/detail on tablet vs single-pane on phone) — swap fragments in/out.
• Multiple screens behind a single Activity — common with the `Navigation` library.
• Reusable UI components needing their own lifecycle hooks (e.g. a permissions flow).

A Compose-first app usually has no Fragments at all: one Activity hosts composable destinations. Fragments remain in View-based codebases and in mixed apps, where a Compose screen is hosted inside a Fragment through `ComposeView`.

Gotchas: Fragments have TWO lifecycles (the fragment and its view) — observe `viewLifecycleOwner` for view-bound state, `this` for fragment-bound state. Null out a view binding in `onDestroyView`, or the fragment keeps the whole destroyed view tree alive.

question: What is an Intent? Explicit vs implicit, and how do you get a result back?
answer:
An Intent is a message describing an operation to perform. Used to:
• Start an Activity.
• Start or bind a Service.
• Send a Broadcast.

Two flavors:
• Explicit — you name the exact component (`Intent(ctx, ProfileActivity::class.java)`). Used for in-app navigation.
• Implicit — you name an action (e.g. `Intent.ACTION_VIEW` plus a URI). The system picks an app that can handle it. Used for sharing, dialing, opening links.

Intents carry data in extras (a Bundle). Keep them small — an oversized extra throws `TransactionTooLargeException`, because the whole thing crosses a Binder transaction.

To get a result back, use the Activity Result API: `registerForActivityResult(contract) { result -> }` at construction time, then `launch(...)`. It replaces `startActivityForResult` / `onActivityResult`, both deprecated, and it survives process death and rotation because the callback is re-registered before the result is delivered.

One trap: since Android 11, package-visibility filtering means `resolveActivity` returns null for apps you haven't declared in `<queries>`, so it is not a reliable "can anyone handle this?" check. Catch `ActivityNotFoundException` around `startActivity` instead.

question: How do you handle configuration changes (rotation) on Android?
answer:
By default, configuration changes (rotation, locale, dark-mode flip, multi-window resize) trigger Activity destruction + recreation. Strategies to keep state:

• ViewModel — survives configuration changes; tied to the ViewModelStoreOwner (Activity / Fragment / NavBackStackEntry). Idiomatic place for screen state.
• `onSaveInstanceState(out: Bundle)` — small Bundle for transient UI state (selected tab, scroll, draft text). Used after process death too.
• `rememberSaveable` (Compose) — wraps the same mechanism for composables.
• `android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize"` — opts out of recreation. Use sparingly: you must handle layout updates manually and miss the recreation flow.
• Saved State Module (`SavedStateHandle` in ViewModel) — persists key/values that survive process death AND rotation.

question: Which parts of an app have to be declared in AndroidManifest.xml rather than in code?
answer:
The manifest is how an app tells the system what it contains, before any of its code runs.

It lives at `app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml` and declares:

• Application-level attributes — name, theme, icon, backup rules.
• Components — `<activity>`, `<service>`, `<receiver>`, `<provider>`. A component that is not declared cannot be started at all.
• Intent filters — which intents each component handles (launcher, deep links, share targets). Anything with an intent filter needs an explicit `android:exported` value.
• Permissions — `<uses-permission>`; dangerous ones still need a runtime request.
• Hardware and software requirements — `<uses-feature>` (camera, NFC), which also drives Play Store device filtering.
• Network security config — cleartext policy, certificate pinning, debug-only trust anchors.

What does NOT belong here: `applicationId`, `minSdk`, `targetSdk` and `versionCode`/`versionName` come from the Gradle build file and are injected at build time.

Gradle merges the main manifest with build-variant and library manifests into one file; when a library adds a permission or a provider you did not expect, the merged result under `build/intermediates/merged_manifests/` and the merger report are where you find it.
code_example:
<!-- AndroidManifest.xml — main pieces -->
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android">

  <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
  <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.CAMERA" />
  <uses-feature android:name="android.hardware.camera" android:required="false" />

  <application
    android:name=".MyApp"
    android:allowBackup="true"
    android:icon="@mipmap/ic_launcher"
    android:roundIcon="@mipmap/ic_launcher_round"
    android:theme="@style/Theme.MyApp"
    android:networkSecurityConfig="@xml/network_security_config">

    <activity
      android:name=".HomeActivity"
      android:exported="true">
      <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
      </intent-filter>
    </activity>

    <!-- Deep link -->
    <activity android:name=".ProfileActivity" android:exported="true">
      <intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" />
        <data android:scheme="https"
              android:host="example.com"
              android:pathPrefix="/u/" />
      </intent-filter>
    </activity>

    <service android:name=".SyncService" android:exported="false" />
    <receiver android:name=".BootReceiver" android:exported="true">
      <intent-filter><action android:name="android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED"/></intent-filter>
    </receiver>

    <provider
      android:name="androidx.core.content.FileProvider"
      android:authorities="${applicationId}.fileprovider"
      android:exported="false"
      android:grantUriPermissions="true">
      <meta-data android:name="android.support.FILE_PROVIDER_PATHS" android:resource="@xml/file_paths"/>
    </provider>
  </application>
</manifest>

question: How do runtime permissions work on Android?
answer:
Android grades permissions by risk, and only the dangerous ones need a runtime request.

• Normal — granted at install time (internet, vibrate). Declaring them in the manifest is all it takes.
• Dangerous — privacy-sensitive (camera, location, contacts). Declared AND requested at runtime, and the user can revoke them later.
• Special — system-managed (overlay, exact alarms, all-files access). No in-app dialog exists; you send the user to a Settings toggle.

The request flow:

1. Declare the permission in the manifest.
2. Check with `ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission` — never assume a previous grant is still there.
3. If not granted, launch the Activity Result contract (`RequestPermission` or `RequestMultiplePermissions`). The old `requestPermissions` / `onRequestPermissionsResult` pair is deprecated.
4. If `shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale` is true, explain why before asking again.
5. On permanent denial the system dialog stops appearing and returns denied immediately, so the only remaining path is a deep link into app settings.

Recent changes worth knowing: POST_NOTIFICATIONS became a runtime permission in Android 13; Android 14 added partial photo access (`READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED`), so a granted media permission may cover only the photos the user picked. Best of all, the Photo Picker needs no permission at all — prefer it over asking for READ_MEDIA_IMAGES.
